meta.audience: Readers of the small plates; within the chapter, the assembled people of Nephi

world_behind.title: The first named opponent in the record
world_behind.text: Everyone who has opposed the prophets so far has been a brother, a brother-in-law, or an unnamed crowd. Sherem arrives from outside the narrative with a name, a program, and a rhetorical method, and the text does not say where he came from, only that "there came a man among the people of Nephi."

world_behind.title: His argument is conservative
world_behind.text: Sherem does not attack the law of Moses; he defends it. The charge is that Jacob has perverted the right way by converting the law into worship of a being who has not come. That is a real objection with a real shape, and it is the objection a strict Mosaic observer would make.

world_behind.title: Learning as rhetorical training
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says he was learned and had a perfect knowledge of the language, and immediately attaches flattery and power of speech to it. In the ancient world mastery of a language usually meant formal training in persuasion. The record's first professional debater is described in the vocabulary of a trained speaker.

world_behind.title: A demand with precedent on both sides
world_behind.text: Gideon asks for proof and receives it; Deuteronomy 6 forbids putting the Lord to the test; Jesus in the wilderness cites that same verse to refuse. Scripture supplies warrant for granting such a request and warrant for declining it, and the chapter puts Jacob on the second side while leaving the outcome to God.

world_behind.title: A deathbed retraction, given publicly
world_behind.text: Sherem calls the assembly himself, announces he will die, and recants before them. Ancient legal practice weighted a dying statement heavily, since a man with nothing left to gain has no reason to lie. The chapter uses that convention without naming it, and the crowd's collapse in verse 21 is the response.

world_behind.title: "Adieu."
world_behind.text: The last word of the book is a French loanword, long naturalized in English by the nineteenth century and ordinary in the American speech of the translation's period. Literally "to God," it is a farewell that commends the hearer rather than merely parting from them, which suits the sentence it ends.

words.text: The aim is announced in a word that belongs to cities and armies. Sherem preaches that there should be no Christ, and the record adds that "this he did that he might overthrow the doctrine of Christ" (v. 2). In the King James Bible the verb is what happens to Sodom, to altars, to armies in the field, and in one of Paul's letters it is what false teachers do to the faith of some. A teaching is being described as a structure that can be pulled down, not as a claim to be argued with.

cites.quote: this he did that he might overthrow the doctrine of Christ

spans.text: this he did that he might overthrow the doctrine of Christ

words.text: "On this wise did he speak unto me" (v. 6) introduces the one long speech Sherem is given. The word is a noun here, meaning manner or way, and has nothing to do with wisdom; Matthew opens his account of the nativity with the same idiom. A reader who has just been told this man was learned can take it for a compliment. It is only the record saying: here is how he put it.

cites.quote: On this wise did he speak unto me

spans.text: On this wise did he speak unto me

words.text: The charge has a legal edge. Blasphemy is speech that injures God, and Leviticus makes it punishable by stoning; the gospels report the same word brought against Jesus for speaking as God speaks. Sherem does not say Jacob is mistaken or confused. He says "this is blasphemy" (v. 7), naming a capital offense under the very law he has just accused Jacob of abandoning. No proceeding follows in the chapter.

To throw into confusion, and in the King James Bible it is what happens to speech at Babel and to enemies in the psalms. Treated at 1 Nephi 2:14. Jacob does not say he persuaded Sherem or answered him. He says he confounded him in all his words, a defeat of the man's speech.

The allegory's verb, and the last chapter used it forty times of God and his vineyard. Here it is what the people do for the man who was struck down: he lay for many days and was cared for. The word makes his final speech possible, and nothing in the text remarks on the irony.

The word means "to God" and offers a commendation. It is the only occurrence in the record and the last word of Jacob's book. He has just said he hopes many of his brethren may read his words, and the word he chooses to end on hands the reader over.

phrases.term: He preached many things which were flattering unto the people
phrases.text: To flatter is to praise falsely in order to gain, and the verb turns up twice in three verses, both times naming the method. Method is stated before content: what Sherem taught gets half a clause, and what made it work gets the rest of the sentence. The record does not say he argued well; it says he pleased, and only the teaching is ever refuted.

phrases.term: He was learned, that he had a perfect knowledge of the language of the people
phrases.text: Learning is granted without qualification and then put next to the power of the devil in the same sentence. Nothing here says education is bad; it says this man's was aimed. The record elsewhere warns about being learned and thinking oneself wise, and this verse is the narrative version of that warning.

phrases.term: He had hope to shake me from the faith... wherefore, I could not be shaken
phrases.text: Jacob's answer is an inventory: many revelations, things seen, angels ministering, the voice of the Lord in very word. He had ended the previous chapter worrying about being shaken from his firmness. Here the word returns and the answer is settled.

phrases.term: Convert the law of Moses into the worship of a being which ye say shall come
phrases.text: The most precise statement of the opposing case anywhere in the record. Sherem is not arguing that God does not exist or that the scriptures are false. He is arguing that a future person has been inserted into a present law, and that no one can speak of things to come.

phrases.term: Believest thou the scriptures? And he said, Yea
phrases.text: The whole exchange turns here. Jacob does not dispute the law or the learning; he establishes shared ground in one question and then says Sherem does not understand what he already accepts. The refutation is about reading.

phrases.term: None of the prophets have written, nor prophesied, save they have spoken concerning this Christ
phrases.text: A universal claim about every prophet who ever wrote, made to a man who has just said he believes it. It is unprovable in the exchange and it is not defended. Jacob simply asserts the reading and moves to his own witness in the next verse.

phrases.term: What am I that I should tempt God to show unto thee a sign
phrases.text: The refusal quotes Deuteronomy's rule about not tempting the Lord (Deut. 6:16), the verse used to end the wilderness temptation. Jacob declines to be the one who asks, and then hands the matter over without specifying an outcome.

phrases.term: Nevertheless, not my will be done... And thy will, O Lord, be done, and not mine
phrases.text: The Gethsemane formula, stated twice in one verse, roughly five centuries before the garden. Jacob puts it around the one moment in his record where he might have wanted something to happen, and the doubling makes it the most careful sentence in the chapter.

phrases.term: He had been deceived by the power of the devil
phrases.text: His own account, given publicly. Sherem does not describe himself as having reasoned badly or as having lied for gain. He describes himself as having been taken in, which is a stranger confession than the one the reader expects and harder to dismiss.

phrases.term: I fear lest I have committed the unpardonable sin, for I have lied unto God
phrases.text: The specific charge he brings against himself is the lie in verse 10. He said he believed the scriptures while denying what they testify. The record's picture of the worst sin is knowingly saying the opposite of what one knows, and the phrase occurs only once more.

phrases.term: Our lives passed away like as it were unto us a dream
phrases.text: The closing self-portrait, and it is bleak. Lonesome, solemn, wanderers, cast out, born in tribulation, hated, mourning out their days. Nothing in it is triumphant, and it is written by the man who had just recorded the vineyard's restoration and the enemy's conversion.

phrases.term: Hoping that many of my brethren may read my words
phrases.text: The plates go to his son, the writing is called small, and the last gesture is toward readers who do not exist yet. Jacob had spent his first chapter worrying that descendants would read with contempt. This is the same worry, resolved into a hope.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: An opponent given a name, a method, and a qualification
verses.text: The record introduces the antagonist with unusual care: "there came a man among the people of Nephi, whose name was Sherem." No origin, parentage, or place is supplied, but verse 4 supplies a credential, "he was learned, that he had a perfect knowledge of the language of the people." The record credits him with an accomplishment before it condemns him, and the accomplishment is linguistic. The two later figures of the same type, Nehor at Alma 1 and Korihor at Alma 30, are introduced the same way, with a name and a skill and no genealogy.

verses.label: v. 9–11
verses.title: A dialogue kept in short alternating turns
verses.text: The record preserves the exchange as question and answer rather than as reported speech. "Deniest thou the Christ who shall come?" draws a two-part reply, "If there should be a Christ, I would not deny him; but I know that there is no Christ." Then "Believest thou the scriptures?" draws a single word, "Yea," which is what the next verse turns against him. Passages built this way, of alternating short turns with the answers preserved, occur only a few times in these books; Alma 11 with Zeezrom is the other extended case.

verses.label: v. 13–14
verses.title: A refusal that contains its own granting
verses.text: The demand is quoted, "Show me a sign by this power of the Holy Ghost," and the reply declines on principle: "What am I that I should tempt God to show unto thee a sign in the thing which thou knowest to be true?" Then, in the same breath, the sign is put in God's hands, "if God shall smite thee, let that be a sign unto thee." The verse closes and opens on the same submission formula, "not my will be done" and "thy will, O Lord, be done, and not mine," which brackets the concession between two refusals to choose.

verses.label: v. 22
verses.title: The writer's own satisfaction recorded
verses.text: The record does not leave the outcome unattributed. It reports the writer's reaction and his part in it: "this thing was pleasing unto me, Jacob, for I had requested it of my Father who was in heaven; for he had heard my cry and answered my prayer." A man's collapse and death are entered as an answered prayer, in the first person, one verse after the crowd falls to the earth. The record makes no attempt to soften the sentence.

chapter.title: The opposing case is stated fairly
chapter.text: Sherem gets two verses of uninterrupted argument, in his own voice, with his best point made: the law has been redirected toward someone who has not arrived, and no one can speak of what has not happened. The record does not caricature him, and readers have found his position more respectable than the narrative treats it.

chapter.title: Jacob's defense is biographical
chapter.text: Asked to hold the faith against a trained speaker, he lists what he has seen and heard. Verse 5 is an inventory, and verse 12 repeats it. Against an argument from the impossibility of future knowledge, he offers the fact of his own experience, which is not a refutation and is not offered as one.

chapter.title: The sign is not produced; it is permitted
chapter.text: Jacob refuses to ask. What he does is submit the question and say twice that he wants God's will and not his own. The distinction matters, because the chapter's model for handling a demand for proof is to decline to be the one who arranges it.

chapter.title: The people he misled look after him
chapter.text: Verse 15 is one clause and it changes everything that follows. Sherem lies for many days under their care, and that care is what makes his confession possible. The record reports it without comment and never returns to it.

chapter.title: The confession is that of a deceived man
chapter.text: Sherem says he was taken in by the power of the devil and that his sin was lying about what he believed. That is a more disturbing account than opportunism, because it does not require him to have been insincere while he was succeeding.

chapter.title: Revival and stalemate are reported together
chapter.text: Verse 23 reports the recovery, "peace and the love of God was restored again among the people; and they searched the scriptures." Verse 24 reports the failure without a break, "many means were devised to reclaim and restore the Lamanites to the knowledge of the truth; but it all was vain." Verse 25 then reports the military consequence, fortifying "with their arms, and with all their might." Two verses separate a spiritual recovery from a stated dead end, and the record supplies no transition between them.

chapter.title: The book ends on grief and a hope
chapter.text: The record of a man who preached a vineyard restored closes with lonesome, solemn, wanderers, cast out, mourning out our days. Then comes a hope that many will read, and "adieu." Jacob does not resolve the two. He sets the summary of his life next to the wish for readers and stops.

applications.title: State the other side accurately
applications.text: Jacob's record gives his opponent two clean verses. Before answering a position you disagree with, try writing it out the way its best defender would.

applications.title: Find the shared premise
applications.text: Jacob's first move is a question whose answer he already knows. When someone disagrees with you, look for what you both already accept and start the conversation there.

applications.title: Refuse to arrange the proof
applications.text: Do not manufacture evidence for someone determined not to be convinced, and do not make the outcome your project. The verse's method is to decline, submit, and leave it.

applications.title: Nourish the person who was wrong
applications.text: The people cared for the man who had deceived them, and that care is what gave him a chance to speak. Consider what it would cost you to look after someone whose position you defeated.

applications.title: Name the specific sin
applications.text: Sherem does not confess in general; he identifies the exact lie. In your own accounting, replace a vague sense of failure with the particular thing you actually did.

applications.title: Say your summary honestly
applications.text: Jacob wrote down the truth about his life without dressing it up and without despairing. Practice describing a hard stretch of your own that way, accurately and without a bow on it.

questions.text: Where am I persuaded by how well something is said rather than by whether it is true?
If someone tried to shake me, what would my inventory actually contain?
What do I say I believe while living as though the opposite were true?
What sign have I been asking for, and would I accept it if it came?
Who have I written off that I could still care for?
If I wrote one honest sentence summarizing my life so far, what would it say?
